Distribution of Pedestrian Fatalities by Roadway Function Class and Land Use (Chang, 2008) 2.2.1.3 Street Lighting and Safety If one of the causes of the high night-to-day accident ratio is the inability of drivers to detect and recognize roadway obstacles and vulnerable road users far away enough to adapt their trajectories, then lighting systems should help target detection at any point of the road surface. The purpose of street lighting is to allow drivers to anticipate emergency situations, and thus to increase accident-avoidance performance (Mayeur, 2010). In fact, street lighting has been proven to be an effective countermeasure against traffic crashes and to reduce crash severity on both rural and urban roads. Through a comparative analysis of more than 3,400 rural intersections along the state’s trunk highway system and a before-and-after 5 analysis of a sample of 12 intersections, Preston and Schoenecker (1999) found that the installation of street lighting in Minnesota reduced both nighttime crash frequencies (25% to 40%) and crash severity (8% to 26%). A benefit-cost analysis using statistics from the before- and-after analysis found that crash reduction benefits associated with the installation of street lighting at rural intersections outweigh the costs by a wide margin. Isebrands et al. (2006) did a comprehensive analysis again to evaluate rural intersections in Minnesota and found that the expected ratio of night to total crashes was 7% higher for unlighted intersections and was statistically significant. A before-and-after analysis of 48 intersections revealed a 13% reduction in night crash frequency and a 36% decrease in the ratio of night-to-day crash rate after lighting was installed. Also, the expected night crash rate before lighting was installed was 59% higher than after lighting was installed. As a result of the analysis, it was concluded that the installation of street lighting at rural intersections is a low-cost and very effective strategy for mitigating nighttime crashes and would likely be far more effective than either rumble strips or overhead flashing beacons. More recently, two studies evaluated the effect of light levels at intersections on night-to-day crash ratios. In the first study (Bhagavathula et al., 2015), average horizontal illuminances at rural intersections in Virginia showed that an increase in the light level by 1 lux was associated in a decrease in night-to-day crash ratio by 7%.
